title: Psicología
blurb: Sesgos, memoria, hábitos, influencia social y emociones.

lessons.title: Trampas mentales
lessons.summary: Los atajos mentales que nos engañan a todos.

cards.title: Dos sistemas
cards.text: El psicólogo Daniel Kahneman describió dos modos de pensar. El Sistema 1 es rápido, automático e intuitivo. El Sistema 2 es lento, costoso y lógico. La mayoría de los sesgos surgen cuando el Sistema 1 responde antes de que el Sistema 2 lo compruebe.

deep.x: Kahneman, a psychologist who won the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics, popularised the labels in his 2011 book *Thinking, Fast and Slow*. The terms "System 1" and "System 2" were first coined by Keith Stanovich and Richard West in 2000. They are a handy metaphor for two styles of thinking, not two separate parts of the brain.
A quick test
Try this before reading on. A bat and a ball cost €1.10 together. The bat costs €1 more than the ball. How much is the ball?

x: Intuition says 10 cents
Check: bat would be €1.10, total €1.20, wrong
Ball = 5 cents, bat = €1.05, total €1.10

deep.x: Shane Frederick used this puzzle in his 2005 Cognitive Reflection Test. Around half of students at top American universities gave the fast, wrong answer. They weren't stupid; System 1 offered an answer that felt right, and System 2 didn't bother to check.
Who does what

System 1 is not the villain. It lets you drive a familiar road, read emotions and catch a falling glass. Experts build excellent intuitions through practice. Problems come when a situation is new, statistical or designed to mislead, and the fast answer goes unchecked.

deep.w: Your brain has a logical half and an emotional half
deep.r: The two systems are a model of thinking styles; real brains mix both everywhere

deep.x: Kahneman later admitted that a chapter of his book leaned on priming studies that have since failed to replicate. The two-systems idea survives; some of its famous examples do not.
System 1 suggests, System 2 is supposed to check, and most errors happen when the check is skipped.

cards.title: Sesgo de confirmación
cards.text: Nos fijamos en la información que coincide con lo que ya creemos, la recordamos y confiamos en ella, y descartamos la que no. Por eso dos personas pueden leer la misma noticia y sentir ambas que tienen razón.

deep.x: Confirmation bias works at every step: what we search for, how we interpret it and what we remember later. It feels like thinking, which is what makes it so hard to spot.
The classic experiments

In 1960 Peter Wason gave people the sequence 2, 4, 6 and asked them to find the hidden rule. Most guessed "even numbers rising by 2" and tested only sequences that fitted, like 8, 10, 12. The real rule was simply "any increasing numbers". People rarely tried a sequence that could prove them wrong.

In 1979 Charles Lord and colleagues showed supporters and opponents of the death penalty the same two studies, one for and one against. Each side rated the study that agreed with them as better designed and found flaws in the other.
Where you meet it

x: Search engines: typing "is coffee bad for you" finds different pages from "benefits of coffee"
Social media feeds that learn what you like and show you more of it
Doctors anchoring on a first diagnosis and reading new symptoms to fit it
Investors who only follow news that supports the shares they already own

deep.w: Correcting someone always makes them believe the myth more
deep.r: The "backfire effect" mostly failed to replicate; corrections usually help a little

deep.x: Ask what evidence would prove you wrong, then go and look for it.

cards.title: Anclaje
cards.text: El primer número que oyes arrastra tu estimación hacia él, aunque sea aleatorio. Una chaqueta «rebajada de 300 € a 120 €» parece barata porque los 300 € se convirtieron en el ancla.

deep.x: Anchoring is one of the most reliable findings in psychology. It shows up in shops, salary talks, courtrooms and property prices, and it works even on experts who know about it.
The wheel of fortune
In a 1974 study by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, people watched a wheel that was rigged to stop at 10 or 65. They were then asked what percentage of United Nations members were African countries.
A number everyone knew was random still moved the answers by 20 points. People adjust away from the anchor, but not far enough.
Why it works
A second reason is that the anchor makes us think of reasons it might be right. Asked "is this house worth €400,000?", you start noticing the good kitchen and the view.
Real-world anchors

x: Price tags with a crossed-out "was" price
The first offer in a negotiation, which often sets the range for the deal
Asking prices for flats in Lisbon or Porto, which shape what buyers think is fair
Sentencing demands: German judges' sentences were swayed by numbers from dice in a 2006 study

deep.x: Large replication projects (Many Labs, 2014) confirmed that anchoring is strong. Effects of truly incidental anchors, like the last digits of an ID number, are smaller and less consistent.
Write down your own number before you hear anyone else's.

cards.title: Heurística de disponibilidad
cards.text: Juzgamos lo probable que es algo según la facilidad con que nos vienen ejemplos a la mente. Los accidentes de avión salen en las noticias, así que volar parece más arriesgado que conducir, aunque por kilómetro es mucho más seguro.

deep.x: A heuristic is a mental shortcut. The availability heuristic swaps a hard question ("how common is this?") for an easy one ("how quickly can I think of an example?"). Usually that works, because common things come to mind easily. It fails when memory is skewed by vivid, dramatic or recent events.
Flying versus driving
Air crashes are rare but get global coverage. Car crashes are common but rarely reported unless local. In the EU, roughly 20,000 people die on the roads each year, about 600 of them in Portugal.
After the 11 September 2001 attacks, many Americans drove instead of flying. Gerd Gigerenzer estimated this led to about 1,600 extra road deaths in the following year.
The letter K test

Tversky and Kahneman asked whether more English words start with K or have K as their third letter. Most said "start with", because those are easier to search for in memory. In fact, words with K in third place are more common.
Everyday effects

x: People buy flood insurance just after a flood, then let it lapse
A friend's burglary makes your area feel unsafe
Shark attacks feel likely after a summer of headlines

deep.w: If I can think of many examples, it must be common
deep.r: Ease of recall reflects media and memory, not frequency

deep.x: When judging risk, look for the base rate, not the headline.

cards.title: Falacia del coste hundido

items.r: «¿Vale la pena de aquí en adelante?»

cards.text: Seguimos invirtiendo en algo por lo que ya hemos gastado, no por lo que está por venir. Terminar de ver una mala película porque pagaste la entrada es un caso clásico.

deep.x: A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent that you can't get back. Logically, only future costs and benefits should guide a decision. Emotionally, walking away feels like admitting a waste.
The theatre experiment

In 1985 Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer gave some theatre subscribers random discounts on season tickets. Those who paid full price went to more plays in the first half of the season. The money was gone either way, but paying more made people feel they had to "get their money's worth".
From cinema seats to supersonic jets

Britain and France kept funding the Concorde long after it was clear it would never pay back. Economists sometimes call this the **Concorde fallacy**. The same pattern appears in failing IT projects, renovations that spiral, and wars that continue "so the dead didn't die in vain".

x: You paid €12 for a film
After 30 minutes it's dull
The €12 is gone whether you stay or leave
The only question: is the next 90 minutes worth more than leaving?

deep.x: Why we fall for it
There are fair reasons to persevere: a reputation for finishing things, or a project close to paying off. The fallacy is only when the past spending itself is the reason.
Seasoned investors have a saying for this: "don't throw good money after bad".
Ask: if I hadn't spent anything yet, would I start this today?

cards.title: Aversión a la pérdida
cards.text: Perder 50 € duele aproximadamente el doble de lo que alegra ganar 50 €. Por eso la gente asume grandes riesgos para evitar una pérdida, pero juega sobre seguro para proteger una ganancia.

deep.x: Loss aversion is the heart of **prospect theory**, published by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979. It says we judge outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point, usually what we have now, and losses weigh more.

x: Coin flip: heads you win €150, tails you lose €100
Expected value = +€25 per flip
Most people still refuse
They need a win of about €200 to accept

deep.x: The endowment effect
In a 1990 study, students were given university mugs. Owners asked about twice as much to sell them as other students would pay to buy them. Simply owning something turns giving it up into a loss.
Where it shapes behaviour

x: Investors hold losing shares too long, hoping to get back to even
Free trials work: cancelling feels like losing something you have
"Avoid a €5 surcharge" motivates more than "get a €5 discount"
Football coaches play safe when ahead and gamble when behind

deep.w: Loss aversion is a fixed law of human nature
deep.r: It varies; for small, routine sums it can be weak, and researchers still debate its size

deep.x: The same €50 counts twice: once as money, and again as a loss or a gain.

cards.title: El efecto Dunning-Kruger
cards.text: Quien sabe un poco suele sobrestimar su habilidad, porque aún no sabe lo que no sabe. A medida que crece la experiencia, la confianza primero baja y luego sube junto con la habilidad real.

deep.x: In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students on logic, grammar and humour. Those in the bottom quarter scored around the 12th percentile but rated themselves around the 62nd. Top scorers slightly underrated themselves.
Why it might happen

Their explanation was a "double burden": the skills you need to do a task well are the same skills you need to judge whether you did it well. A beginner at grammar can't spot their own grammar errors.
The debate

The effect is more contested than its fame suggests. Part of the pattern appears even with random data, because almost everyone rates themselves "above average" and extreme scores drift towards the middle when measured again. Studies that correct for this still find a modest effect, but much smaller.

items.r: Low scorers overrate a bit more
Internet meme, not in the paper

deep.x: The famous curve with "Mount Stupid" and a "valley of despair" was never in the original paper. It is a popular cartoon of the idea. Confidence does often wobble while you learn a skill, but that's an observation about learning, not what Dunning and Kruger measured.

deep.w: Dunning–Kruger proves that stupid people think they're geniuses
deep.r: Almost everyone overrates themselves a little; beginners just have more room to be wrong

deep.x: Feedback from reality is the cure, because you can't judge a skill you don't yet have.

cards.title: Sesgo de supervivencia

items: quien dejó la carrera y triunfó

cards.text: Estudiamos a los ganadores y olvidamos los fracasos que no vemos. «Deja la universidad como los fundadores famosos» ignora a los miles que la dejaron y no tuvieron éxito.

deep.x: Survivorship bias happens when we only see the cases that made it through some filter and treat them as the whole picture. The failures are missing, so the lessons we draw are wrong.
The bomber planes

In the Second World War, the US military studied bombers returning from missions and mapped the bullet holes. The obvious plan was to add armour where the holes were. Statistician Abraham Wald pointed out the opposite: the planes hit in other places, such as the engines, never came back.
More everyday cases

items.b: only the sturdy ones still stand

deep.x: "They don't build them like they used to" is often survivorship bias. The badly built houses from 1900 were demolished long ago; only the best remain.
The founder myth

Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg left university, but most successful founders didn't. A 2018 study of US start-ups found that the average age of founders of the fastest-growing firms was about 45, and most had degrees and years of experience.
Funds that close are often dropped from databases, so the average fund looks better than the funds investors actually held. Analysts must correct for this to get honest figures.
Before learning from winners, ask where the losers went.

cards.title: El efecto marco
cards.text: El mismo dato se percibe distinto según cómo se formule. Los pacientes eligen mucho más a menudo una cirugía con un «90 % de supervivencia» que una con un «10 % de mortalidad», aunque sean idénticas.

deep.x: A frame is the way a choice is presented. Logically, two descriptions of the same fact should lead to the same decision. In practice, frames that stress losses push people towards risk, and frames that stress gains push them towards safety.
The disease problem
In a famous 1981 study, Tversky and Kahneman described a disease expected to kill 600 people. People chose between a sure option and a gamble, described either in lives saved or lives lost.
The two sure options were identical. Only the wording changed, and the majority flipped.
Framing all around you

x: "75% lean" mince sells better than "25% fat"
"Save €200 a year" versus "lose €200 a year by not insulating"
A 1982 study found doctors were also swayed by survival versus death framing

deep.x: Defaults are frames too

Portugal is one of several European countries with an opt-out system for organ donation since 1993: you are a donor unless you register to refuse. Countries with opt-out defaults tend to have far more registered donors than opt-in ones, although actual donation rates also depend on hospitals and families.
Showing both frames side by side, or using natural numbers ("10 out of 100"), greatly reduces the framing effect.
Before deciding, restate the choice the other way round and see if you still agree.

cards.title: Vencer tus sesgos

items: Fija tu presupuesto antes de ver precios

cards.text: No puedes desactivar los sesgos, pero sí ir más despacio en las decisiones importantes: busca pruebas en contra, pregúntate «¿qué me haría cambiar de opinión?» y decide antes de ver el ancla.

deep.x: Knowing about biases helps less than you'd hope. Emily Pronin found in 2002 that people readily spot biases in others but see themselves as objective, a **bias blind spot**. The trick is not willpower but changing the process you use for decisions that matter.
Tools that work
The **pre-mortem**, proposed by psychologist Gary Klein, asks a team to imagine the project failed a year from now and explain why. It makes it safe to voice doubts.
Build guardrails

x: Set your budget or price limit before you look at offers, so the anchor is yours
Use checklists, like pilots and surgeons do
Ask a friend to argue the other side
Keep a decision diary: write down what you expect, then check later

deep.x: The EU gives you 14 days to cancel most online purchases. That's a built-in pause for System 2 to catch up with an impulse buy.
In forecasting tournaments run by Philip Tetlock, one hour of training in simple techniques like base rates improved accuracy by around 10%.
You can't remove biases from your head, but you can design decisions so they matter less.

quiz.q: Una tienda anuncia «antes 300 €, ahora 120 €». ¿Qué sesgo hace que parezca barato?
Mantener una mala inversión por lo que ya pagaste es la…
quiz.explain: Solo importan los costes y beneficios futuros.

quiz.q: ¿Cuánto más duele, más o menos, una pérdida que una ganancia equivalente?
quiz.explain: Aversión a la pérdida, medida por Kahneman y Tversky.

lessons.title: Cómo funciona la memoria
lessons.summary: Por qué olvidas y cómo recordar mejor.

cards.title: Tres etapas
cards.text: La memoria tiene tres etapas: codificación (captar la información), almacenamiento (conservarla) y recuperación (volver a sacarla). La mayor parte del «olvido» es en realidad un fallo al codificar o al recuperar.

deep.x: The three-stage model goes back to Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin in 1968. It's a simplification, but it helps you diagnose why something was forgotten: was it never taken in, did it fade, or is it there but out of reach?
Encoding failures

You have seen thousands of €1 coins, but could you draw one accurately? In a 1979 study, Americans were asked to pick the correct penny from 15 drawings and fewer than half managed it. They had never encoded the details, because they never needed to.
How deeply you process something matters. Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart showed in 1972 that thinking about a word's meaning leads to much better memory than noticing its letters or sound.
Retrieval failures

The tip-of-the-tongue feeling proves a memory can be stored but temporarily unreachable. You might know the first letter and the number of syllables, yet the word won't come. It often pops up later, once the right cue appears.

x: Cues help: the smell of a school corridor can bring back a whole year
Retrieval practice makes paths easier to find next time
Stress and tiredness make retrieval harder, which is why exam blanks happen

deep.w: Forgotten memories are erased
deep.r: Many are still stored; what's lost is the route back to them

deep.x: To remember something, make sure it gets in deeply and practise getting it out.

cards.title: Corto plazo frente a largo plazo
cards.text: La memoria de trabajo retiene solo unos pocos elementos durante segundos, unos 4 bloques. La memoria a largo plazo no tiene prácticamente límite y puede durar toda la vida.

deep.x: In 1956 George Miller wrote a famous paper about "the magical number seven, plus or minus two". Later research by Nelson Cowan suggested the true limit is closer to about four meaningful chunks.
A workbench, not a box
Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed in 1974 that short-term memory is really a **working memory**: a mental workbench where you hold and juggle information.

The phonological loop is the inner voice repeating a phone number. The sketchpad holds images and routes. The central executive directs attention. That's why it's hard to do mental maths while someone talks to you: both compete for the same limited space.
The patient H.M.

In 1953 Henry Molaison had parts of both hippocampi removed to stop severe epilepsy. His short-term memory still worked; he could chat normally. But he could no longer form new long-term memories of facts and events. Yet he improved at a mirror-drawing task over days, without remembering practising. He showed that memory is not one single system.
Long-term memory lasts
Harry Bahrick tested people's Spanish 50 years after school. Much was lost in the first few years, but what survived then stayed stable for decades. He called it "permastore".
Without rehearsal, information in short-term memory fades within about 20 seconds.
Working memory is a tiny desk; long-term memory is a vast library, and learning is the job of moving things from one to the other.

cards.title: La curva del olvido
cards.text: Hermann Ebbinghaus demostró en 1885 que olvidamos rápido: gran parte del material nuevo desaparece en un día si no lo repasamos. Cada repaso aplana la curva.

deep.x: Ebbinghaus was a German psychologist who used himself as the subject. He memorised lists of meaningless syllables like "DAX" or "BUP" so prior knowledge couldn't help. Then he measured how much time he saved relearning them later.
What the curve shows
Forgetting is steepest at the start and then slows. Most of the loss happens in the first hours. What remains after a month tends to stay for a long time.
In 2015 Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros repeated the experiment and got a very similar curve, so this is one of psychology's oldest results that has held up.
Why reviews flatten it
Each successful review makes the memory more stable, so the next decline is slower. After several spaced reviews, a fact can last months or years.
Caveats

x: Nonsense syllables are the worst case; meaningful material fades more slowly
Things linked to what you already know are forgotten far less
Skills like cycling or swimming barely follow the curve at all

deep.w: If you forget something, you never really learnt it
deep.r: Forgetting is normal; a quick relearn is much faster than the first time

deep.x: Expect to forget fast, and plan reviews for it.

cards.title: Repetición espaciada
cards.text: Repasar justo antes de olvidar es la forma más eficiente de aprender. Los intervalos crecen cada vez: 1 día, 3 días, una semana, un mes. La cola de repaso de esta app usa la misma idea.

deep.x: The **spacing effect** is one of the most replicated results in learning research, confirmed in hundreds of studies since Ebbinghaus. The same total study time works much better spread out than crammed together.
Why waiting helps

When you review just as a memory begins to fade, the effort of retrieving it strengthens it more than an easy review would. Cramming feels productive because everything is fresh, but that fluency fades within days.
How big should the gaps be?

A large 2008 study by Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues found that the best gap depends on how long you want to remember. For a test in a week, a gap of about a day worked well; for remembering a year later, gaps of about three to four weeks.
From card boxes to apps

x: 1972: Sebastian Leitner's system of flashcards in boxes; correct cards move to a box reviewed less often
1987: Piotr Woźniak's SuperMemo computes intervals for each card
Today: apps like Anki and this one schedule reviews automatically

deep.x: The spacing effect also works for babies, older adults and even animals; it seems to be a basic property of how memory works.
Little and often beats a lot at once, as long as the gaps keep growing.

cards.title: Recuerdo activo
cards.text: Ponerte a prueba es mejor que releer. Intentar sacar una respuesta de la memoria la refuerza mucho más que volver a mirarla, incluso cuando te equivocas.

deep.x: Retrieval doesn't just measure memory, it changes it. Each time you pull something out, the route to it gets stronger. Psychologists call this the **testing effect**.
The key study
In 2006 Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students learn a passage. Some reread it four times; others read it once and then tried to recall it three times.
Five minutes after studying, the rereaders did slightly better. A week later the result reversed. Rereading creates a feeling of familiarity, which is easily mistaken for knowing.
Ways to do it

x: Close the book and write down everything you remember
Use flashcards with the question on the front
Explain the idea out loud as if teaching a friend
Try practice questions before you feel ready

deep.x: Mistakes are useful
Getting an answer wrong and then seeing the correct one still helps, as long as you get feedback. Even guessing before you study a topic can make the later lesson stick better.

deep.w: Testing is just for measuring what you know
deep.r: Testing is one of the best ways to learn it in the first place

deep.x: If it feels effortful to recall, the effort is the learning.

cards.title: Agrupación
cards.text: Recordamos más si agrupamos los elementos en bloques con sentido. Un número de teléfono como 912345678 es más fácil como 912 345 678, y los maestros de ajedrez ven patrones en el tablero, no piezas sueltas.

deep.x: A chunk is a group of items that your memory treats as a single unit. Because working memory holds only about four chunks, making each chunk bigger lets you hold far more.

x: 9 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 = 9 separate digits
"FBI CIA EU" = 3 chunks, though it's 8 letters

deep.x: Chess masters

In 1973 William Chase and Herbert Simon showed chess positions for five seconds. Masters could rebuild real game positions almost perfectly, while beginners placed only a handful of pieces. With random positions, the masters' advantage almost vanished.
Masters didn't have better memories; they had thousands of familiar patterns stored in long-term memory, so each pattern became one chunk.
Expertise is chunking

A runner known as S.F. trained in 1980 to raise his digit span from about 7 to about 80. He did it by turning digits into running times he knew, such as "3:49.2, near a mile record". His span for letters stayed at about 7.
Chunking in daily life

x: Your IBAN is printed in blocks of four
Musicians read chords, not single notes
Learning common phrases in a language beats learning single words

deep.x: The same trick works for skills: practised movements become one chunk, so a driver changes gear without thinking about each step.
Memory isn't about holding more things, it's about making each thing bigger.

cards.title: Sueño y memoria
cards.text: Durante el sueño profundo, el cerebro reproduce las experiencias del día y las traslada al almacenamiento a largo plazo. Pasar la noche en vela antes de un examen perjudica justo los recuerdos que necesitas.

deep.x: Sleep isn't downtime for memory. During the night the brain sorts, strengthens and links what you learnt during the day, a process called **consolidation**.
Replay in the night

In 1994 Matthew Wilson and Bruce McNaughton recorded neurons in rats running a maze. During later sleep, the same cells fired again in the same order, as if the rats were rehearsing the route. Similar replay has since been found in humans.
Different sleep stages, different jobs
Most deep sleep comes early in the night, and most REM sleep comes towards morning. Cutting sleep short at either end costs you something.
Before and after learning

x: Sleep after learning protects new memories from interference
Sleep before learning matters too: a tired brain encodes new information less well
Even a short afternoon nap can improve recall of material learnt that morning
A 1924 study found people forgot less over 8 hours of sleep than 8 hours awake

deep.w: You can catch up on sleep before an exam at the weekend
deep.r: Missed consolidation on the nights after learning isn't fully recovered later

deep.x: The night after learning is part of the lesson.

cards.title: Recuerdos falsos
cards.text: Los recuerdos se reconstruyen cada vez que los evocamos, así que pueden cambiar. Elizabeth Loftus demostró que una pregunta tendenciosa («¿a qué velocidad iban los coches cuando se estrellaron?») altera lo que recuerdan los testigos.

deep.x: Remembering is not like replaying a video. Each time you recall an event, your brain rebuilds it from fragments, filling gaps with expectations, later information and imagination. The rebuilt version is then stored again.
Car crash experiment
In 1974 Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed people films of car accidents and asked how fast the cars were going. Only one verb in the question changed.
A week later, about a third of the "smashed" group remembered seeing broken glass. There was none.
Planting whole events

In the 1990s Loftus and colleagues convinced about a quarter of adults that as children they had been lost in a shopping centre. Other studies planted memories of hot-air balloon rides, using doctored photos.
Why it matters

x: Eyewitness mistakes played a role in about 70% of US convictions later overturned by DNA evidence
Police lineups in many countries now follow rules to avoid suggestive questions
Vivid "flashbulb" memories, like where you were for a shocking event, change over the years while confidence stays high

deep.w: A vivid, confident memory must be accurate
deep.r: Detail and confidence can grow even as accuracy falls

deep.x: Memory is a reconstruction, not a recording, so treat even your own with some humility.

cards.title: El palacio de la memoria
cards.text: Una técnica antigua: imagina un lugar conocido y coloca cada cosa que quieras recordar en un punto de un recorrido. Al recorrerlo mentalmente, las cosas vuelven. Los campeones de memoria la usan.

deep.x: The **method of loci** (Latin for "places") is said to come from Simonides of Ceos in ancient Greece. According to Cicero's retelling, a banquet hall collapsed and Simonides identified the victims by remembering where each had sat. Roman orators used the technique to deliver long speeches without notes.

steps: Put a vivid image at each spot

deep.x: Why it works
It uses two things the brain is very good at: remembering places and remembering strange images. A plain list has no structure, but a route provides ready-made order and cues.

x: Shopping list: eggs, olive oil, bread
Front door: eggs cracking on the doormat
Hallway: slipping on a pool of olive oil
Kitchen: a loaf of bread singing fado

deep.x: Evidence

In 2017 Martin Dresler and colleagues trained ordinary people in the method for 30 minutes a day over six weeks. Their recall of a 72-word list rose from about 26 words to about 62. Brain scans showed their brain connections becoming more like those of memory champions.
Limits

x: It's best for ordered lists, names, numbers and speeches
It doesn't create understanding, so use it alongside learning the meaning
You can reuse a palace, but old images can interfere with new ones

deep.x: Memory champions generally don't have unusual brains; studies find that their skill comes from training techniques like this one.
Your brain remembers places and pictures far better than lists, so turn lists into places.

cards.title: Un plan de estudio que funciona
cards.text: Combina los trucos: sesiones cortas, ponte a prueba, espacia los repasos y duerme. Diez minutos al día con esta app valen más que dos horas una vez a la semana.

deep.x: In 2013 John Dunlosky and colleagues reviewed ten popular study techniques. Only two were rated "high utility": practice testing and spreading study over time. Highlighting, rereading and summarising were rated low, even though they're what most students do.
Put it together

x: Keep sessions short, 10–30 minutes, with a clear goal
Start each session by recalling last time's material before looking at notes
Mix topics and problem types instead of doing all of one kind (**interleaving**)
Stop well before bedtime and protect your sleep
Plan A: 120 minutes once a week
Plan B: 10 minutes a day = 70 minutes a week
B uses less time
B gives 7 retrievals and 7 nights of sleep in between

deep.x: Why the small daily habit wins

Daily practice turns each session into a spaced review. Every return to the material is a test of memory, and the gaps grow naturally as you move on. A long weekly session mostly helps in the first hour, then you're rereading what's already fresh.

deep.w: Feeling confident after a long study session means you've learnt it
deep.r: Fluency right after study fades fast; delayed recall is the real test

deep.x: Short, spaced, self-tested and slept on: that's how learning lasts.

quiz.explain: El recuerdo activo supera al repaso pasivo.
